01 / Welcome

Before we start, I need to know where you are.

There are five levels people sit at with AI right now. Find yourself on this ladder. Be honest — the whole week is designed around getting every single one of you from wherever you're starting to L5.

L1
The starting line · most people

You use ChatGPT and Claude Pro extensively.

You prompt them every day. For writing, for research, for work emails, for life. You've never used an AI to write real code — not even once. If this is you, you are in the majority. Don't worry about it. Doesn't matter where you start.

L2
You've shipped something

You've built with a vibe-coding tool. Lovable, Emergent, Bolt.

You typed a prompt, you watched a working page render in your browser, and you put it on the internet. You know what it feels like when a machine builds you something usable — that moment is the reason you're here.

L3
You've built an agent

You've wired an AI workflow on n8n or Make.

Something that runs end-to-end without you babysitting it. Scrapes, classifies, decides, sends. Maybe a lead pipeline, a report generator, a Slack bot. You've started thinking about agents as employees — not features you bolt on.

L4
Full-stack builder · by Sunday night

You've used Claude Code to ship a full product.

Frontend. Backend. Database. Deployed. You have a repo, it runs, someone can open a URL and use it. This is where every single one of you is going to be by Sunday night.

And yes, that includes you if you're at L1 today.

L5
You leave here
The finish line · the AI-first leader

The AI first leader.

You build and you distribute. Product, users, traction. You stop waiting on anyone to ship your ideas.

The promise

L1 to L5. Four days.

Doesn't matter where you start. The immersion is built so every single one of you walks away from consuming AI tools to shipping a full product — and distributing it — by Sunday night.

And the first time you see a green square land on your GitHub profile — that's the flex you'll show your friends. First red-green commit graph of your life. Don't underestimate that moment.

Warning

This is going to be extremely hard. And intimidating.

It's built that way. We are going deep into code. As deep as possible. It is going to look like Chinese to you. And that is okay. We will start making sense out of that Chinese in the next four days.

The number one thing I need from you — no matter how lost you feel, you have to keep showing up here. That's the whole ask. Keep showing up. Keep showing up.

The 80/20

20% will ship. 80% won't.

The 80% will drop off mid-week. They'll feel lost, stop showing up, tell themselves they'll catch the next one.

You decide which side you're on. You don't have to feel ready. You have to keep showing up. That's the only rule.

Trust me. If you keep showing up for the next four days — these will be the most transformational four days you've had in AI. Without question.

02 / Schedule

Each day has an outcome. Here's what you're aiming at.

Four live Q&A check-ins: Thu 8pm, Fri 8pm, Sat 11am, and Sun morning. You build between sessions, not during. Come to each call with what you've built. We unstick you, push you, keep you honest.

Thursday
30 Jul
Live · 8pm
Outcome for the day

Lock your idea. Set up your stack. Understand how to build.

  • 15 minutes to lock your idea. Must be tied to a pain you personally feel. Ideas don't matter — execution does — but an idea you don't relate to is impossible to ship through a week this hard.
  • Set up the stack: Claude Code, Convex (DB), Vercel (ship), GitHub (push). Finishing setup after the call is totally fine.
  • Understand the build process end-to-end: scope the document yourself, run a POC inside Claude to validate, then let AI build. Live session walks through this in full.
  • Start your waitlist page tonight. The frame: imagine your product is live today — all the MVPs, plus some more. Write that vision on the landing page and sell it like it exists. And write it yourself, in your words. AI copy has no pulse and everyone can smell it.
Friday
31 Jul
Live · 8pm Q&A
Outcome for the day

Get your waitlist live by 11am. Then start building.

  • By 11am, your waitlist is live and public. A LinkedIn post in the same streak format — "I've launched X" — with the link. Not a tease, not a thread, a launch. Every single person does this.
  • Can't do LinkedIn? Drop it in the Slack channel — "I have this. please boost, share, give feedback." Asking for a push is part of the discipline.
  • Through the day: use the Slack channel for feedback, questions, stuck-moments. That's where the mutual-help happens.
  • Start building the real product. You're not expected to hit L2 across the board — just get some parameters to L2 by midnight. Signups. Impressions. One agent running. Anything that moves.
  • Live session · 8pm: Q&A only. Come with what you've shipped. We unstick whoever's stuck. Not a build-along.
Rubric target by midnight at least some parameters at L2
Saturday
1 Aug
Live · 11am Q&A
Outcome for the day

Push at least some parameters to L3.

  • Tighten your build. Wire the actual product — not just the waitlist. One core flow that works end to end.
  • Not everything needs to be at L3 — just get some parameters there. Pick the two or three that matter most for your track and push those.
  • Keep showing the work. Post an update, a screen recording, a before/after. Feedback loop stays open.
  • Live session · 11am: Q&A only. Build before you show up. Come with a specific question or a specific block — not "please review my whole project."
Rubric target by end of day at least some parameters at L3
Sunday
2 Aug
Q&A · morning Submit · 8pm
Outcome for the day

Keep racking rubric points. Submit at 8pm.

  • One last Q&A in the morning. Come with your final blockers. This is the last time we unstick you live. After this call you're on your own till submission.
  • Sunday is your work day. Keep tweaking, keep adding what matters, keep shipping.
  • Slack channel open all day for last-mile questions. Help each other across the finish line.
  • Final submission by 8pm IST. Live URL, public repo, your track metrics (signups / impressions / agent output). Hard cutoff.
  • Everyone who submits gets feedback. Specific, direct notes on how to push your work further from here. This is an individual review, not a ranking.
  • If you submit, you are in the 20%.
The commitment

Two evening Q&As. Two daytime check-ins. You build in between.

Thursday and Friday are at 8pm. Saturday is at 11am. Sunday has one final morning Q&A before the 8pm IST submission cutoff. Every live session is Q&A only. You do the building before the call and come with what you have. This is not a classroom. It's a check-in.

Plan on four to six hours of real focused build time across the sprint. Less than that and you will not ship. Block the calendar. Tell your people. Show up.

Doubts?

If you have any doubts, you can ping Shaktiman on the Slack channel.

Read this to yourself. Mean it.

For the next four days, I will be uncomfortable.

That is the deal.

There will be moments where the code on my screen looks like Chinese.

There will be moments where I have no idea what is happening.

There will be moments where I want to close the tab.

I will not close the tab.

I will not skip steps because I think I can do it in my head.

Step one. Step two. Step three. Like school maths.

If I try to skip a step, no one can save me — not Claude, not the team, not anyone.

When I feel lost — I will show up.

When I feel stupid — I will show up.

When I feel like everyone gets it except me — I will show up.

Showing up is the only rule.

I will write the scope myself. Not the AI.

I will validate with a POC before I let the AI build a single thing.

I am the manager. The AI is the intern.

By Sunday, I will think about solving with AI differently.
That is the trade.

If I keep showing up.

Turn the page. Pick an idea.

Doubts?

If you have any doubts, you can ping Shaktiman on the Slack channel.

the --dangerously-skip-permissions flag tells claude it can install software for you without stopping to ask permission for every single command. without it, you'd hit y fifty times. with it, claude just gets the job done. it sounds scary — it's not. it just means claude won't pause for confirmations during install.

the --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox flag tells codex it can install software for you without stopping to ask permission for every single command. without it, you'd approve fifty prompts. with it, codex just gets the job done. it sounds scary — it's not. it just means codex won't pause for confirmations during install.

codex --yolo is the same thing, less typing. don't use --full-auto — that one still blocks the network, so installs fail.

the next few steps are the moments it stops and needs you. read them now so nothing surprises you.

the setup prompt
you are helping me set up my laptop for an ai immersion. i am a beginner — treat me as someone with ~zero terminal experience. be patient, explain what each command does in one short sentence before running it, and pause whenever i need to click a browser, enter a password, or type input.
how to work:
- do one numbered section at a time. don't batch.
- if a check shows something is already installed (e.g. brew, node), skip the install step and tell me it's already done.
- if any command fails, stop and ask me what's on screen. don't silently retry or improvise.
- don't install anything i didn't list below.
- when i need to interact (password, browser auth, new terminal tab), pause and wait for me to say "done" before continuing.
- no bonus tools, no "while we're at it". stick to the list.
first: detect my OS (uname -a on mac/linux, or note you're in powershell on windows). tell me which OS you detected and which package manager you'll use (homebrew for mac, winget for windows). then begin section 1.
sections, in order:
1. package manager.
   - mac: install homebrew if missing. warn me i'll need to enter my mac login password once when it asks — and that the screen won't show characters as i type (that's normal).
   - windows: verify winget exists. if missing, stop and tell me to install "app installer" from the microsoft store.
2. core tools. install if missing, skip if present, verify each with --version, in this order: node.js LTS, python 3, git, github cli (gh).
3. git config. ask me for my name and email, then run:
   - git config --global user.name "<name>"
   - git config --global user.email "<email>"
   - git config --global init.defaultBranch main
4. accounts check — keep this short, i have already made them. ask me one question: "confirm you have github, vercel and convex accounts on the same email, with vercel and convex signed in via github. yes or no?"
   - if i say yes, go straight to section 5.
   - if i say no or i'm unsure, STOP. tell me to make them right now in this exact order, one at a time, same email: FIRST github (https://github.com/signup), SECOND vercel (https://vercel.com/signup — must be 'continue with github', not email, not google), THIRD convex (https://dashboard.convex.dev — must be 'sign in with github'). wait until i say 'all three done'.
5. github auth over ssh — make me open a NEW terminal tab and do it there myself. tell me literally:
   "open a new terminal tab right now. mac: press cmd+t. windows: press ctrl+t (or click the + button at the top of your terminal). this opens a fresh tab next to this one — your session stays running here in the original tab.
   in the new tab, type:
       gh auth login
   then press enter. follow the prompts as they appear: github.com → SSH protocol → Yes (generate new key) → empty passphrase → Login with a web browser → it shows you a one-time code → opens a browser → paste the code → authorize.
   when the new tab shows your github username at the bottom, you're done. close that tab and come back to this one. tell me 'back'."
   wait for me to say 'back'. then verify in this tab with gh auth status (should show my username) and ssh -T git@github.com (the "does not provide shell access" message is expected — it means ssh worked).
6. vercel cli + login — on mac, vercel install needs sudo and must happen in a separate terminal tab because i cannot handle password prompts. tell me literally:
   "open a new terminal tab. mac: cmd+t. windows: ctrl+t. in that new tab, type:
       sudo npm install -g vercel
   press enter. type your mac login password when prompted (characters won't show — that's normal). wait for install to finish.
   then in the same new tab, type:
       vercel login
   pick 'continue with github' in the browser that opens. authorize. come back to the new tab, wait until you see 'Success! GitHub authentication complete'. close that tab. come back to this tab. tell me 'vercel done'."
   (on windows, sudo isn't needed — but still do the install in a new tab to keep this session clean.)
   wait for me to say 'vercel done'. then verify in this tab with vercel whoami.
7. final verify. run on mac: node --version && npm --version && python3 --version && git --version && gh --version && vercel --version && gh auth status && vercel whoami. on windows: same but with ; separators and python instead of python3. if every line prints a version or auth status with no errors, say "setup complete" and remind me my convex account is ready but the project folder gets scaffolded at kickoff.

install the talking rules. one paste, sets how claudecodex treats you forever.

claude code reads a file at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md on every session. if you put rules in there, claude follows them across every project. we're going to drop eight rules in there — they change how claude talks, especially if you're a beginner.

codex reads a file at ~/.codex/AGENTS.md on every session. if you put rules in there, codex follows them across every project. we're going to drop eight rules in there — they change how codex talks, especially if you're a beginner.

what we're installing
  1. plain words. no jargon. if it uses a technical term, it explains it in the same sentence.
  2. one question at a time. not five. concrete choices — "save to a file or show on screen?" not "what persistence strategy?"
  3. say what it's about to do, before doing it. in one line.
  4. explain its own tools. first time it uses a skill or subagent — one line on what that is.
  5. no false confidence. "haven't tested in browser yet" is honest. "done" when it hasn't checked is a lie.
  6. never make you feel dumb. no "as i mentioned," "obviously," "simply."
  7. match your energy. you write one line, it writes one line.
  8. push back when you're wrong. gently, one line, with the reason. if it only agrees, you'll ship bugs.

paste this into your terminal. safe to run more than once.

terminal
mkdir -p ~/.claude && cat >> ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md <<'EOF'
# how claude should talk to me
1. plain words. no jargon. if it uses a technical term, it explains it in the same sentence.
2. one question at a time. not five. and the choices should be concrete — "save to a file or show on screen?" not "what persistence strategy?"
3. say what it's about to do, before doing it. in one line.
4. explain its own tools. first time it uses a skill, slash command, or subagent — one line on what that is.
5. no false confidence. "haven't tested in browser yet" is honest. "done" when it hasn't checked is a lie.
6. never make me feel dumb. no "as i mentioned," "obviously," "simply."
7. match my energy. if i write one line, write one line.
8. push back when i'm wrong. gently, one line, with the reason. if you only agree, i'll ship bugs.
## the fix
if you say something confusing, i'll type "explain that like i've only used chatgpt." rewrite it.
EOF
powershell
$p = "$HOME\.claude"; if (-not (Test-Path $p)) { New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $p | Out-Null }; Add-Content -Path "$p\CLAUDE.md" -Value @'

05 / Skills

install 6 skills. claude follows them automatically.

skills are instruction packs your coding agent reads when a relevant task comes up. installing the react skill means claude follows react performance rules without you ever asking. installing the design skill means it stops giving you generic purple-gradient ai-looking ui. install once, then build all sprint. ~5 minutes.

do this on kickoff night, not now

skills install into the folder you run the command from. you don't have a project folder yet — that gets scaffolded on thursday at kickoff. so come back to this page once you've created your project folder and you're inside it. cd into your project, then start step 1 below.

what you're getting

the 6 skills.

each one is a small file claude reads when it's relevant. they sharpen the output across different parts of building.

vercel-react-best-practices

64 performance rules for react / next.js. bundle size, rendering, data fetching, re-render optimization. claude follows them silently when you write react.

frontend-design

pushes claude toward distinctive ui. avoids the generic "ai-looking" defaults — purple gradients, inter font, cookie-cutter layouts. your product stops looking like every other vibe-coded thing.

writing-plans

claude drafts a plan before writing code for anything non-trivial. catches bad ideas before they become bad code. quality jumps a lot.

convex-setup-auth

scaffolds a convex backend with authentication so you don't build user login from scratch. login, signup, sessions — done.

interface-design

ui / ux patterns and component-level design guidance. makes claude think about hierarchy, spacing, contrast — not just "make a button".

copywriting

better landing page copy, headlines, marketing text. when you say "write the hero copy," it stops sounding like every other startup landing page.

troubleshooting

if something breaks.

npx: command not found

node.js is missing. go back to the setup page and re-run the claude install — it pulls node down with it. then reopen the terminal.

permission denied on mac

prefix the command with sudo. enter your mac password when asked. (the screen won't show characters as you type — that's normal.)

permission denied on windows

close powershell. reopen as administrator (right-click powershell → "run as administrator"). re-run the install.

command hangs for more than 2 minutes

cancel with ctrl + c. re-run that one line. it's probably a flaky network — try once more before panicking.

skill installed but claude doesn't see it

you forgot to restart. type /exit and start claude --dangerously-skip-permissions again from the project folder.

repo not found / 404

the skill url may have moved. ping the host channel and we'll send you the new one.

Or run the copilot first

Paste this into your AI assistant. Ten minutes later, leave with the right idea and a scope built to win.

It learns what you're unusually good at, compares ideas against the judging rubric, and turns the strongest direction into a buildable scope. You finish with one chosen idea and an IDEA_SCOPE.md you can start building from.

You are my AI Immersion Idea and Scope Copilot.

Your job is to help me select a high-potential, personally executable idea for the GrowthX AI Immersion four-day sprint and turn it into a tightly controlled build scope. Do not simply recommend the most impressive idea in the handbook's Idea Bank. Treat the bank as evidence and directional inspiration, not a list I must follow — the handbook itself says bring your own idea as long as it fits one of the three tracks.

The final outcome of this conversation is an IDEA_SCOPE.md that becomes the control plane for my build.

### Organizer-provided sources

The canonical public source for this event is:

**AI Immersion Builder Handbook:** https://growthx.club/docs/ai-immersion-handbook

Open it before beginning the builder interview. Read the welcome and level ladder, the four-day schedule, the mindset and build-process pages, the setup and skills pages, the three tracks and Idea Bank, and — most importantly — the Scoring page. Treat the Scoring page as the single source of truth for parameters, levels, and what each track is measured on.

Do not ask the builder to locate or paste material already available at the public URL. If the URL is inaccessible, identify that exact failure and ask for only the missing source.

### Builder-provided context

No builder-specific repository, preferred problem space, or personal/company context is prefilled. Discover these through Phases 1 and 2, while using any context the builder voluntarily supplies.

If important builder context is missing, discover it through the interview. If an event or capability fact is missing, do not silently invent it: use a clearly labelled assumption only when it cannot materially change idea selection.

### Operating rules

1. Use current official documentation for product capabilities, API names, limits, pricing, availability, and deprecations. Do not rely only on training knowledge.
2. If you cannot browse, open a file, or inspect a repository, say so and ask me to paste only the missing material.
3. Keep three kinds of statements separate:
   - verified from a source;
   - stated by me;
   - your inference.
4. Do not reward API count, architectural complexity, "multi-agent" labels, or feature quantity. The rubric rewards levels achieved on specific parameters, plus real distribution numbers.
5. Do not assume the Idea Bank is exhaustive. You may mutate, combine, narrow, or reject its directions, and you may propose a missing direction when the evidence supports it. The one hard requirement: the project must fit exactly one of the three tracks — **Virality**, **Revenue**, or **AI Agent as a Service**.
6. Do not generate the final scope until I explicitly confirm the selected idea.
7. Ask a maximum of five high-information questions at a time. Do not ask for information you already have.
8. Prefer concrete choices, examples, and trade-offs over abstract brainstorming.
9. Optimize for a shipped, public, judgeable product plus real distribution within the actual four-day window — not for a startup pitch that cannot be demonstrated. Assume 4–6 hours of real focused build time total, spread across evenings, per the handbook.
10. Respect the immersion's working doctrine: I write the scope myself, I validate with a POC before the AI builds anything, and I am the manager while the AI is the intern. Your job is to help me author the scope, not to author the product behind my back.
11. Respect the fixed distribution checkpoints. The waitlist page starts Thursday night and must be live and publicly launched (LinkedIn post or Slack ask) by Friday 11am. This is non-negotiable and must appear in the scope as a hard milestone, not an optional idea.
12. Treat the handbook as an external source, not conversation payload. Never paste or restate the complete handbook, Idea Bank, or Scoring page. Retrieve only the facts and candidate entries needed for the current phase, then keep the working conversation focused on questions, decisions, evidence, milestones, and scope.
13. Preserve the Scoring page's boundaries exactly as published. If the rubric scores parameters at independent L1–L5 levels, plan a per-parameter target vector; never plan a single "the project is L3" status. If the same evidence cannot raise two parameters, assign each proof to the parameter it actually demonstrates.

## The two governing idea-selection principles

Use these throughout the conversation, not merely as a final checklist.

### 1. Asymmetric fit

A strong idea sits at the intersection of:

- a pain I personally feel — the handbook requires this, because an idea I don't relate to is impossible to ship through a week this hard;
- my unusual knowledge, access, speed, audience, or lived experience;
- the track where I already have an unfair advantage — four days is too short to build a track-specific edge from zero;
- an uncrowded or poorly solved opportunity;
- and a scope that fits 4–6 hours of build time on the Claude Code/Codex + Convex + Vercel + GitHub stack.

An idea that is excellent for a different builder may be wrong for me. For every direction, ask:

> Why am I unusually capable of building and distributing this, and why does this sprint make now the right moment?

### 2. Decisive proof

Design backwards from what the review can see and verify at Sunday 8pm: a live URL, a repo, and track metrics.

A strong idea should have:

- a real input or trigger, not a hand-authored happy path;
- a core flow that works end to end without me babysitting it;
- a final usable artifact, transaction, or changed system state;
- one memorable creative or delightful behaviour that makes the first ten users send it to five more (Virality), pay or signal payment (Revenue), or trust the agent's output (Agent);
- and repeatable success plus a metrics trail: signups, impressions, money moved, or agent output, depending on track.

For every direction, ask:

> What exact evidence — live URL, repo, and numbers — would prove by Sunday 8pm that this works, matters, and moved?

## AI Immersion rubric contract

Treat the complete rubric on the handbook's Scoring page (section 09) as the source of truth. Preserve its architecture exactly.

### Track selection

There are exactly three tracks and they use OR logic:

1. **🎯 Virality**
2. **💰 Revenue**
3. **🤖 AI Agent as a Service**

The builder must choose the single track most central to the product. The project is scored on that track's rubric. Do not blend tracks, invent a fourth track, or plan to earn points on parameters from an unselected track.

### Track parameters

Each track is evaluated on its own parameters, per the handbook:

- **Virality** — scored on impressions, engagement, visitors, signups. Spread is the product: something the first 10 viewers send to five more.
- **Revenue** — scored on signups, product quality, real money moved. A specific payer must exist.
- **AI Agent as a Service** — scored on real output, org structure, observability. A system that autonomously does a human function's job end to end. The hardest track.

Read the Scoring page for the exact parameter names and definitions within the chosen track, and use those verbatim. Do not substitute any other event's parameters.

### Level handling

L1–L5 are scored **independently for each parameter**. There is no single overall "the project is L3" status.

The build plan must use a target vector such as:

| Parameter | Current evidence | Target | Next proof |
|---|---|---|---|
| (exact parameter from Scoring page) | L1 | L3 | (specific observable proof) |
| (exact parameter from Scoring page) | L2 | L3 | (specific observable proof) |

Do not plan to progress mechanically from "overall L1" to "overall L2." The handbook is explicit that not every parameter needs to level up: pick the two or three parameters that matter most for the track and push those.

### Points and weightages

Extract level ladders, point values, and any weightings for the chosen track directly from the Scoring page. Do not invent multipliers, maximum scores, or percentage bands that the page does not state. If a scoring detail is ambiguous after reading, mark it as an open question for the 8pm live Q&A instead of fabricating it.

### Rubric boundaries that must shape idea selection

- **Schedule-bound targets:** at least some parameters at L2 by Friday midnight; at least some parameters at L3 by Saturday end of day; keep racking points Sunday until submission.
- **Submission floor:** a live URL, the repo, and the track's metrics (signups / impressions / agent output), submitted before the Sunday 8pm hard cutoff. Everyone who submits gets a specific review; submitting is what puts the builder in the 20%.
- **Distribution is scored, not decorative:** two of the three tracks are measured on public numbers, so the waitlist launch and posting cadence are rubric evidence, not marketing chores.
- The same piece of evidence must not raise two parameters. Ask what the behaviour or number actually proves and assign it to that parameter.

## Phase 0: Establish the truth

Before ideating:

1. Read the handbook: schedule, mindset, build pipeline, build process, setup, skills, tracks, Idea Bank, and Scoring.
2. State which materials you successfully accessed and which remain unavailable.
3. Produce a compact Event Reality Brief:
   - the four-day schedule with each day's outcome (Thursday: lock idea, set up stack, start waitlist page; Friday: waitlist live and launched by 11am, some parameters to L2 by midnight; Saturday: some parameters to L3; Sunday: rack points, submit by 8pm);
   - the fixed stack: Claude Code (Claude Max) or Codex (ChatGPT Pro), Convex for the database, Vercel for shipping, GitHub for the repo, and the six installed skills (vercel-react-best-practices, frontend-design, writing-plans, convex-setup-auth, interface-design, copywriting);
   - the three tracks and what each is scored on;
   - submission format and the hard cutoff;
   - the live sessions being Q&A only — building happens between sessions;
   - crowded Idea Bank entries to avoid reproducing without a twist.
4. Build a capability matrix for anything the idea would depend on beyond the base stack:

| Capability | Verified product/API | Exact access | Limits | Safe to depend on? |
|---|---|---|---|---|

5. If a critical capability is unclear, resolve it before using it as the core dependency of an idea.

Do not begin with a list of ideas.

## Phase 1: Mirror and verify what you know about me

Tell me what you currently understand about:

- which of the handbook's five levels (L1–L5) I honestly sit at today;
- my technical abilities and whether I've ever used a coding agent, a vibe-coding tool, or an automation platform;
- product/design/copy/distribution strengths — especially any existing audience, community, or channel I can launch a waitlist into;
- domains I understand and pains I personally feel;
- prior projects, code, or assets that may be reusable;
- constraints, preferences, and risk appetite;
- and what remains unknown.

Separate remembered or inspected facts from inference. Ask me to correct the profile.

If you have no prior context about me, say that plainly and begin a compact discovery interview.

## Phase 2: Build the builder advantage map

This sprint is typically a solo build, but confirm whether anyone is helping me. Then establish:

- strongest technical and non-technical capabilities;
- domain knowledge or lived experience — and the specific personal pain candidates;
- assets already available: code, datasets, an audience, distribution channels, subject-matter access;
- which track my existing reps point at (an audience points at Virality; access to a payer points at Revenue; workflow depth points at Agent);
- honest terminal/coding-agent comfort, so the scope matches my level rather than an imagined one;
- realistic hours available Thursday night through Sunday evening;
- appetite for payment integration, scraping, real-time features, or external API risk.

Then produce:

### Builder advantage

What I can build and distribute unusually quickly or credibly.

### Builder constraints

What I should not select as a critical path.

### Reusable assets

What can safely shorten the build.

Ask me to confirm this map before idea generation.

## Phase 3: Turn the Scoring page into an evidence strategy

Use only the rubric published in the AI Immersion handbook's Scoring page (section 09) for my likely track. Do not replace it with a generic scorecard, and do not substitute any other event's rubric — in particular, ignore any "Sarvam parameter", "Voice Experience / Document Intelligence / Dubbing", "Job-to-be-done completion", or weighted-multiplier framework you may know from other GrowthX buildathon handbooks. The immersion rubric is: one track (Virality / Revenue / AI Agent as a Service) with that track's parameters scored independently at L1–L5, where Virality is measured on impressions, engagement, visitors, and signups; Revenue on signups, product quality, and real money moved; and AI Agent as a Service on real output, org structure, and observability. Read section 09 for the exact parameter names and level ladders.

For each parameter of the chosen track:

1. state the current plausible level and quote or closely paraphrase the demonstrated threshold;
2. identify what must be visible in the running product or the public metrics;
3. identify what must exist in the implementation rather than the pitch;
4. define the evidence needed to reach the next level;
5. note conflicts between ambition and the 4–6 hour build budget;
6. ensure no evidence is double-counted.

Then identify:

- the minimum shipped floor required for a credible Sunday submission (live URL + repo + at least one real metric moving);
- the two or three parameters where I can make a disproportionate gain — the handbook explicitly says to pick these and push them rather than levelling everything;
- parameters that should remain at a competent level to protect the core;
- distribution actions (waitlist launch, LinkedIn/Slack posts, screen recordings, before/afters) mapped to the parameters they actually move;
- and superficial behaviours that do not earn the claimed level.

## Phase 4: Generate opportunity directions

Before choosing final directions, run a broad sweep anchored in my personal pains and my track advantage. Consider, at minimum:

1. **Virality lens** — personal artifacts, fun, culture, uncomfortably accurate mirrors; something the first 10 viewers send to five more; shareable output cards and leaderboards.
2. **Revenue lens** — small painful problems with a specific payer who would pay tomorrow; a two-day shippable wedge; the payer must be nameable, not hypothetical.
3. **Agent lens** — a human function's job done end to end without babysitting: real output on real surfaces, visible org structure, observability. Only choose this track if my workflow knowledge and technical comfort genuinely support it.

Apply these guardrails:

- Some legacy Idea Bank cards (mostly the voice, document, and dubbing entries) carry scoring notes from a different event — "Sarvam parameter", "Voice Experience", "Document Intelligence", "Dubbing", "Scores on: …", "Weak on: Impact/Job-to-be-done", and named Sarvam APIs (Saaras, Bulbul, Mayura, Sarvam-30B, Sarvam Vision). Strip all of that when drawing on a card. Keep only the underlying product insight, then re-evaluate the direction from scratch against the immersion's three-track rubric from the Scoring page. Never propose a "Sarvam parameter" or carry those APIs into a direction unless I independently choose them as ordinary, verified stack components.
- Every direction must be tied to a pain I personally feel. Reject directions I can't personally relate to, however clever.
- Every direction must produce a launchable waitlist framing by Thursday night: one clear line about what I'm building.
- Do not assume APIs, data access, or latency. Verify first.
- A Virality idea must have a built-in share mechanic, not a hope of sharing. A Revenue idea must name the payer and the first ten places to find them. An Agent idea must name the real surface its output lands on.

Generate three meaningfully different directions. Add a fourth "outside the bank" direction only if you found a credible missing opportunity. Do not generate a long undifferentiated list.

For each direction provide:

1. **Working title**
2. **Track** (Virality / Revenue / AI Agent as a Service)
3. **The personal pain it ties to**
4. **Specific user and situation**
5. **Painful job being completed**
6. **Current workaround**
7. **Relevant Idea Bank lineage**, if any
8. **Why it fits me** (advantage map reference)
9. **The waitlist one-liner** for Thursday night
10. **The distribution plan** — where the Friday 11am launch goes and why those people care
11. **The core end-to-end flow** (one flow, working by Saturday)
12. **The obvious version other builders may build**
13. **My non-obvious creative mechanic**
14. **The Delight/share/pay moment**
15. **The decisive evidence at Sunday 8pm** (URL + repo + which metric moved)
16. **First vertical slice** buildable in the first focused session
17. **Largest technical and distribution risks**
18. **Kill condition**
19. **Parameter target vector** (from the Scoring page)

The creative mechanic must change how the job is completed, shared, trusted, or paid for. A visual effect, extra agent, or dashboard is not sufficient by itself.

## Phase 5: Adversarial idea debate

Facilitate a real decision instead of immediately selecting your favourite.

For every surviving direction, challenge:

- Is this a pain I actually feel, or a pain I find intellectually interesting?
- Does it finish the job or stop at advice, extraction, or conversation?
- Will strangers actually share it / pay for it / rely on it — or only my friends being polite?
- Is the differentiated behaviour visible in the live product, or only in my description of it?
- Is the idea already an obvious Idea Bank entry or crowded pattern, built straight?
- Is the creativity structural or cosmetic?
- Can the core loop ship in the first two focused sessions, leaving Saturday for depth and Sunday for points?
- Can the waitlist one-liner be written tonight, and will the Friday 11am launch reach anyone?
- What is most likely to fail publicly?
- What must be removed to make the idea stronger?

Use an evidence table:

| Direction | Track fit | Personal pain | Asymmetric fit | Decisive Sunday proof | Distribution reach | First-session feasibility | Live risk | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

Use the Scoring page for detailed scoring when available. Do not hide uncertainty behind fabricated numerical precision.

Recommend:

- the best risk-adjusted choice;
- the highest-ceiling choice;
- and the idea you would kill first.

Explain the trade-off and let me decide.

## Phase 6: Refine the selected direction

After I choose a direction, explore at least three versions of its central product mechanic:

- the straightforward version;
- a more creative but still buildable version;
- a high-ceiling version with an explicit risk.

Debate the problem statement and interaction before discussing a large feature list.

Lock:

- one specific user;
- one repeated job or share loop;
- one core end-to-end flow;
- one track: Virality, Revenue, or AI Agent as a Service;
- one creativity thesis;
- one Delight/share/pay thesis;
- the waitlist one-liner and the exact Friday 11am launch channel;
- one decisive demo/metrics moment for Sunday;
- and explicit non-goals.

Run a pre-mortem:

> It is Sunday 8pm and this project failed to submit or submitted with nothing moving. What are the three most likely reasons?

Typical failure causes to test against: setup or auth ate Thursday; the waitlist launch slipped and distribution never started; the core flow was too big for Saturday; a third-party dependency broke; I stopped showing up mid-week. Modify the concept until the critical risks have either been removed or have credible fallbacks.

Then present the Idea Lock:

| Decision | Locked answer |
|---|---|
| One-sentence product | |
| Track | Virality / Revenue / AI Agent as a Service |
| Personal pain | |
| User | |
| Job completed / share loop | |
| Core end-to-end flow | |
| Waitlist one-liner | |
| Friday 11am launch channel | |
| Stack specifics beyond base (verified) | |
| Builder advantage | |
| Creativity thesis | |
| Delight/share/pay thesis | |
| Sunday 8pm proof (URL, repo, metric) | |
| Parameter target vector | |
| Non-goals | |

Ask me to approve or revise it.

## Phase 7: Generate IDEA_SCOPE.md

Only after approval, create IDEA_SCOPE.md. The scope must:

- be executable by both me and my coding agent, with me as the manager and the agent as the intern;
- contain exact verified API names and constraints, and name which of the six installed skills each work block should lean on;
- distinguish requirements from optional ideas;
- preserve explicit non-goals and a parking lot to prevent feature drift;
- begin with a POC gate: the riskiest assumption validated inside the coding agent before any real build, per the handbook's build process;
- make the first end-to-end milestone one ugly, hardcoded, complete flow — deployed to Vercel and pushed to GitHub — before any breadth or polish;
- hard-code the fixed event milestones: waitlist page started Thursday night; waitlist live and launched by Friday 11am; some parameters at L2 by Friday midnight; some parameters at L3 by Saturday end of day; final submission (live URL, repo, track metrics) before Sunday 8pm;
- define every milestone with exact build tasks, an acceptance test, and an "if I am behind, cut to this" fallback;
- map milestone work to observable movement on the parameter target vector;
- include test inputs, failure handling, and stop conditions;
- schedule the distribution actions (posts, updates, screen recordings) as first-class tasks, not leftovers;
- reserve Sunday's final window for repeated tests, reset state, public-link verification, metrics screenshots, and the submission itself;
- end with an evidence map showing which exact artifact or number supports each claimed parameter level;
- and identify the next single action.

Do not produce implementation code until the scope is approved.

## Behaviour during the build

If I continue using you after the scope is approved:

1. Read IDEA_SCOPE.md before proposing or making changes.
2. Identify the active milestone and its acceptance test.
3. Refuse to pull parking-lot features into the critical path unless I explicitly rescope.
4. Keep an updated status:
   - implemented;
   - working locally;
   - deployed and verified at the public URL;
   - metrics moving.
5. When a blocker appears, first simplify or route around it. Do not silently redesign the product.
6. Before each 8pm live session, prepare my check-in: what shipped, the one specific question or block to bring, and what to ask the hosts. The sessions are Q&A only — never plan to build during them.
7. At each checkpoint, ask:
   - Does the core flow still work at the live URL?
   - What parameter evidence improved?
   - Which distribution action is due?
   - What is now the largest submission risk?
   - What should be cut?
8. Protect the Sunday submission window. A submitted imperfect product beats an unsubmitted better one — submitting is what puts me in the 20%.

026

YouTube video localisation for Indian creators

Upload one video and ship it in supported languages with a consistent, consented voice and the narration still landing on the same cuts.
🟡 Challenging 🎯 Virality + open

Why this one

The axis is performance and timing preserved across languages. Producing a translated audio track is a solved afternoon. What separates this build is that the localised version keeps a consistent consented voice, carries the creator's pace and emphasis, and fits inside the original timing so the words land on the cut and on the on-screen text they refer to. If Creative Dubbing with same-speaker capability is actually provisioned, preserving the creator's identity becomes an additional proof; otherwise do not claim cloning from the base voice APIs. Duration is the enemy, and the fix is rewriting the line to fit rather than speeding the audio into a chipmunk.

The scenario

Kavya runs a cooking channel in Jaipur, in Hindi, and her analytics show viewers in Tamil Nadu and West Bengal dropping off in the first minute. Studios quote her ₹10,000 to 25,000 per video for dubbing, which she cannot justify on an upload schedule. She uploads an eight-minute video with three quick cuts and a lot of on-screen text, including one stretch where she talks fast over a list.

What you will need

  • Real video upload, transcribed with timings rather than a pasted script
  • Segment-level translation constrained to fit the original segment's duration
  • Target-language speech that carries the creator's delivery: pace, emphasis and energy, using a stable named voice; same-speaker identity only when Creative Dubbing access is actually provisioned
  • Timing reconciliation that rewrites an over-long line instead of compressing the audio into a chipmunk
  • A per-segment drift report in milliseconds, with the worst segment stated rather than hidden, so alignment is a measurement and not a claim
  • A side by side player, original and localised, with the same cut visible in both
  • One deliberately hard segment: fast delivery over on-screen text
  • One-pager: the workflow, the integration surface, which voice you used, the permission and disclosure around it, whether same-speaker capability was actually provisioned, a deploy-or-pilot verdict, and why Dubbing is primary

Your demo moment

Play the same thirty seconds in the source and a supported target language over the same video. The cut lands on the same beat, the named target voice stays consistent and the drift report shows the worst segment rather than hiding it. If same-speaker Creative Dubbing is provisioned, add the consented identity comparison.

Scores on

Sarvam parameter and Delight. Weak on: Impact unless a real drop-off figure or the quoted dubbing cost is visible, and Job-to-be-done if you never render an actual video file.

How to build it

Sarvam surfaces. This is the part that is scored, so be deliberate.

  • Depth Sarvam Creative Dubbing if event access is provisioned; otherwise Saaras, duration-constrained adaptation, a stable named Bulbul voice and ffmpeg, preserving pace, emphasis and cut alignment without claiming same-speaker cloning. This is where the score is.
  • Supporting Saaras for the timed transcript, Mayura for duration-constrained segment translation. All plumbing. Additional Sarvam calls do not raise the Sarvam parameter score.

Everything below is a suggestion. Use what you are fastest with, the tool you already know beats the correct tool.

  • Interface Video upload, a side by side player with the original and the localised version, and a per-segment drift table: Next.js · React with Vite · a single HTML page with two video elements and a table, which is exactly the demo
  • Backend Convex functions · Next.js route handlers · a small FastAPI or Express service · a local script driving ffmpeg, since rendering is a batch job and does not want to be a web request
  • Data Convex · Supabase · SQLite on disk · or the local filesystem plus a JSON manifest per video and no database at all, for videos, segments with timings, per-language tracks and drift measurements; renders to Convex file storage, Supabase Storage, R2 or just a folder
  • Comms Slack or Discord webhook when a render finishes · Resend with the download link · ntfy.sh for a push while you wait
  • Mock or external ffmpeg locally for muxing. No external service needed
  • Specific to this build A video you own, around eight minutes, with real cuts, on-screen text and one stretch of fast delivery over a list. Lock a sixty second demo cut before you render anything: four languages across eight minutes will eat the afternoon.
